reason: The sources provide over a dozen multi-sourced, verifiable facts detailing Gliese 436 b's discovery, exotic ice physics, atmosphere, and evaporating tail.
story: In 2004, astronomers discovered Gliese 436 b, a Neptune-sized exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf star in the constellation Leo. Circling its star in just 2.6 days at a blistering distance of only a few million miles, the world is baked by intense stellar radiation. Yet scientists calculated something bizarre: despite temperatures reaching hundreds of degrees, the planet was predicted to hold solid water ice. Crushing gravitational compression deep within the planet forces water into exotic, dense crystalline phases that cannot vaporize. Nicknamed the planet of burning ice, Gliese 436 b gets even stranger. Ultraviolet observations from the Hubble Space Telescope revealed that intense stellar radiation is actively stripping the planet's atmosphere away, trailing an enormous comet-like hydrogen cloud stretching fifty times the size of its parent star. Further chemical analyses found its atmosphere is packed with carbon monoxide while missing expected methane.
angle: Intense planetary gravity forces water into exotic solid ice at hundreds of degrees Fahrenheit while the planet bleeds a comet-like tail fifty times wider than its star.

claims.claim: The discovery team included astronomers R. Paul Butler and Geoffrey Marcy.
Gliese 436 b was originally detected using the radial velocity method.
Gliese 436 b has a mass and radius comparable to Neptune.
Gliese 436 b orbits a red dwarf star.
The host star Gliese 436 is located in the zodiac constellation Leo.
Gliese 436 b completes one full orbit around its star in about 2.6 days.
Gliese 436 b orbits at an extreme proximity to its star, far closer than Mercury is to the Sun.
Subsequent transit observations confirmed Gliese 436 b's size and orbital characteristics.
Intense gravitational pressure on Gliese 436 b forces water to remain in solid ice phases despite extreme temperatures.
Stellar radiation is causing the atmosphere of Gliese 436 b to evaporate into space.
The evaporating hydrogen atmosphere forms a trailing comet-like cloud roughly 50 times the size of the parent star.
The escaping atmospheric cloud was observed using the ultraviolet capabilities of the Hubble Space Telescope.
Astronomers estimate Gliese 436 b has lost up to 10 percent of its atmosphere.
Gliese 436 b's atmosphere is severely deficient in methane compared to standard equilibrium expectations.
The atmosphere of Gliese 436 b contains an unexpectedly high abundance of carbon monoxide.

disputed: Surface temperature: S1 and S2 report around 439 degrees Celsius (822 degrees Fahrenheit), and S4 reports equilibrium/dayside temperatures between 594 K and 663 K, whereas S3 claims 4,400 degrees Fahrenheit. A script should cite ~800 degrees Fahrenheit / 439 degrees Celsius and discard S3's extreme outlier.
Distance from Earth: S4 cites 32 light-years while S3 cites 43 light-years. A script should either omit distance or attribute 32 light-years based on modern astronomical archives.

Specific ice phase: S2 cites Ice VII, S3 asserts superionic ice, and S1 mentions general exotic high-pressure ice forms. A script should frame specific phases as theoretical or hypothesized forms of high-pressure ice.

Necessity of an ice interior: S1 notes that refined radius models allow a hydrogen-helium envelope over rock without requiring an exotic ice mantle, so a script should present the burning ice mantle as an initial prediction or hypothesis.
